newsitem.title: BELGIUM: FEATURE - LIBERALISATION OF EU SINGLE AIR MARKET.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - LIBERALISATION OF EU SINGLE AIR MARKET.

text.p: Next year's liberalisation of the European Union's aviation sector looks set to be slower than expected with hoped-for cheaper fares and increased competition among airlines coming only gradually.
While EU officials and aviation experts agree the effects of liberalisation are already apparent, they differ on the exact causes and on whether changes are coming fast enough.

"There has been no dramatic decrease in fares, no spectacular disappearance of major carriers, no substantial penetration of domestic markets by foreign competitors," European Commission official Philip Lowe told a symposium of the European Aviation Club.

"Whilst the effects of liberalisation are now noticeable, they are appearing slowly," said Lowe, chief aide to European Transport Commissioner Neil Kinnock. For others, even that position is an overstatement.
"It's very premature to make any assessment of the impacts of liberalisation because we ain't got it yet," Hugh Welburn, economic advisor to Virgin Atlantic, told the same conference.

From April 1, next year, skies above the EU's 15 member countries will be fully liberalised, meaning that airlines based within the bloc may fly freely between the airports they choose offering tickets subject to few price controls.
The date is somewhat academic in that it marks the last step in a process, spanning several years, during which most of the legal barriers to cross-border competition have already fallen.
Given that time frame, air travellers faced with stubbornly high ticket prices, could be forgiven their disappointment.

Lowe said that since 1990, fares on intra-EU routes had dropped five percent on average, albeit with larger falls on those routes served by several airlines. He singled out domestic routes in Germany, France and Italy as ones where fares remained very high compared with the United States, where deregulation took place in the late 1970s.
FULLY FLEXIBLE FARES STILL EXPENSIVE

While discounts exist, via travel agents and for business clients, many travellers would prefer more, fully flexible, low-priced fares such as those offered by Britain's Virgin Express Europe, Easyjet and France's Air Liberte, he said.

"The fact remains that the fully flexible fare between the main airports of Europe remains a pretty expensive commodity. On some routes our analysis shows that fully flexible fares are significantly higher than can be justified by costs."
Lowe said the Commission could use its competition powers to force a reduction of fares on routes "where there is reluctance to take action".
Aside from any Commission action, another factor eroding prices should come from the wider market effects of the new entrant, low-fare airlines.

Keith McMullan, managing director of aviation analyst Avmark International, told the conference that while new airlines offered only two percent of the EU's available scheduled seats, the market effect of their low fares was considerable.

Citing a U.S. Department of Transport study on deregulation, McMullen said: "The impact of low-cost carriers is clear, or as clear as these analyses can ever be: in cities now served by low-cost carriers, passengers pay on average $54 less per flight or $70 less if the city is a (major airline's) hub."
With action to prevent predatory pricing by larger operators, such effects could be emulated in Europe, he added.
U.S EXAMPLE NOT SUITABLE FOR EUROPE
That being said, McMullan warned that the U.S. experience was not where Europe's deregulated market was heading.

Firstly, Europe has a highly developed charter market, which offers 23 percent of the region's available seats, McMullan said. Europe's market is also highly fragmented both by its physical geography and the number of national borders in an area similar to that of the United States's truly single market.
McMullan pointed to Latin America, where there is not a single majority-owned state airline, as a possible model.
Another could be the markets in southeast Asia, where many governments have encouraged second-tier carriers to compete with the traditional incumbents.

Other blips on the Commission's liberalisation radar include the EU executive's ongoing studies of cash injections and accompanying restructuring plans for Air France, Greece's Olympic Airways, Spain's Iberia and Italy's Alitalia.

"I don't think that we can say that the state-aided sector will slide peacefully to its close. We are going to be faced with a considerable degree of hard talking over the next six months," Lowe said.
State aid to government-owned airlines has prompted endless complaints, and legal action in the case of Air France, by the EU's privatised airlines and by the smaller independents.

Welburn said aid was a major stop on competition. "The fact is that European air fares are so high that any moderately competent airline can fly European international routes profitably. Subsidies are completely unnecessary. With no benefits and several disadvantages, they amount to an appalling waste of money," Welburn said. He cited this issue, along with market dominance of Europe's major carriers and new airlines' limited access to landing and take-off slots, as the main barriers to full liberalisation.
As far as slots are concerned, the Commission is planning to propose in November a system which is likely to allow some form of trade in slots.
While liberalisation for airlines is undoubtedly under way, progress with similar efforts in the air services sector is less advanced.
Common EU rules for airport charges, ground-handling services and air traffic control -- all areas with a major impact on airlines' bottom-line costs -- remain some years off.
